subject: chemistry
question_text: What is Pauli's exclusion principle? Give an example.

verification.note: Chapter 1 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.48-52), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The principle
lines: Pauli's exclusion principle: no two electrons
in an atom can have the same set of all
Two electrons in one orbital must differ in s.
steps.why: The first three quantum numbers n, l and m describe the orbital. Two electrons in the same orbital already share all three, so only the spin quantum number is left to make them different.
common_mistakes: Writing three quantum numbers instead of four.
Saying no two electrons can have the same quantum numbers, without the words all four.
steps.memory_tip: Same orbital means n, l and m already match. Only the spin can differ.
steps.margin_note: The phrase all four quantum numbers is the whole mark.

steps.label: The example
lines: First electron:  n = 1, l = 0, m = 0, s = +½
Second electron: n = 1, l = 0, m = 0, s = −½
They differ only in the spin quantum number.
steps.why: Helium is the smallest atom with a filled orbital, so it shows the principle with the fewest electrons. Writing the two sets side by side makes the single difference visible.
common_mistakes: Giving both electrons s = +½, which is the arrangement the principle forbids.
Naming an element but not writing out the four quantum numbers.
steps.memory_tip: Write the two rows one under the other. Only the last column changes sign.
steps.margin_note: A small table of n, l, m, s for the two electrons is the fastest way to write this.

insider_note: The question asks for an example in its own wording, so a statement alone can only score half. Helium with the two quantum-number sets written out is the complete answer.
